- If sentiment is consistently positive (≥0.67) over recent days, model tends to overestimate prices; reduce forecast slightly.
- If sentiment is negative (≤-0.5) or volatile, model often underestimates; adjust upward, especially if price is trending down.
- After a sharp price spike (e.g., +5%+ in 3-5 days), model frequently overshoots; cap forecast at 1-2% above peak or use lagged mean.
- When sentiment shifts from positive to negative, model often fails to correct quickly; apply mean reversion to 10-15 day average if sentiment turns negative.
- If model forecast is >10% above recent 10-day average, reduce by 10-20% if sentiment is neutral or negative.
- For 30-day horizon, if true outcome is >15% above forecast, check if sentiment was bullish; if yes, model may have overconfidently assumed continuation; adjust downward 5-10%.
- If sentiment is mixed (±0.3–0.6), model often averages out; use weighted average of recent 7-day mean and 14-day trend for correction.
- If forecast is consistently below true outcome (e.g., 3-5 consecutive days), model may be underestimating volatility; increase by 2-5% if sentiment is bullish.
- If sentiment is high but price is flat or declining, model may overreact; reduce forecast by 3-5% to avoid “sentiment-driven overcorrection.”
